title: The CBAM Policy Tool
subtitle: Measuring exporters' exposure to the EU carbon border adjustment, and what domestic policy can do
message: At €80 a tonne, Turkish hot-rolled steel declared at the default owes €107 a tonne in 2026 and €252 at full phase-in, close to half its price. Where a country has no default of its own, as Egypt has none for steel, verified emissions data are the biggest lever.

problem.title: The charge is large and arrives early

problem.text: Since January 2026 EU importers of steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity owe certificates for embedded emissions. Emissions above the benchmark are charged in full from the first year.

mechanism.title: Data and a domestic price both cut the charge
mechanism.caption: Turkish hot-rolled steel, €80/tCO₂: default, verified data, and data plus a €20 credited price.
points: Filing data at the country average saves €58 a tonne (the mark-up).
A €20 domestic price saves €49 a tonne and keeps the money at home.
Egypt's gas-based steel would be charged at the 'other countries' default of 4.05 t/t.

action.title: Verify first, then price at home
results: Most exposure arrives in 2026 for goods far above the benchmark.
A rebated domestic price forfeits the Article 9 credit.
Egypt: €418m a year saved by verification, €262m of it on steel.
todo: Build verification capacity at the plants that export to the EU.
Then consider a domestic carbon price on CBAM goods.
Press for revised defaults in the 2027 review.
Use it for exposure, not for a firm's compliance filing.
